tree-sitter-cli 0.24.7 --abi 14 for the ABI-14 runtime), following the
existing grammars/dart pattern. Drop the primary-constructor and
collection-expression masks the new grammar makes unnecessary; keep
preprocessor-line masking and the dictionary index-initializer mask
(non-literal keys still mis-parse), and add a mask for prefix
dereference of pointer casts ('*(T*)&x'), the one remaining unsafe
construct the grammar rejects. Task.cs now parses with zero ERROR
nodes.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Entire-Checkpoint: 60eb72eb08f4

* sem(csharp): infer receiver types from out-declarations and nullable locals

'if (map.TryGetValue(key, out HttpConnectionPool? pool))' followed by
'pool.SendAsync(...)' emitted no CALLS edge: parameterVarTypes mapped
the modifier keyword ('out') as the variable name, and localVarTypes
had no pattern for argument-position out-declarations or
nullable-annotated locals at all.

Strip C# parameter modifiers (out/ref/in/params/this/scoped/readonly)
and the nullable '?' in type-first signatures, and teach localVarTypes
two capitalized-type-first declaration shapes: 'out Type? name' and
'Type? name;'. Name-first languages (Go) cannot match either pattern.

Repro from dotnet/runtime HttpConnectionPoolManager.SendAsyncCore.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Entire-Checkpoint: 5d646f990b6b

* sem(csharp): resolve static calls across partial-class declarations

'Contract.ThrowIfFalse(...)' emitted no edge in roslyn: the receiver
type lookup probed only the lexically-first type declaration with that
short name. Contract is a partial class declared in both
Contract.InterpolatedStringHandlers.cs (sorts first, holds only the
nested handler structs) and Contract.cs (holds ThrowIfFalse), so the
method lookup failed and the call was dropped. The qualified-name tier
could not save it either — ThrowIfFalse has three overloads, so it is
not globally unique.

Resolve type names through typeLikeNamedWithMethod, which prefers the
declaration that actually defines the called method (same-file first,
then any, walking the supertype chain) before falling back to the old
prefer-file pick. Applies to both typed-receiver and static
type-qualified calls.

# GitHub Flavored Markdown Generation

**Version:** 1.2.1

Generate GFM that passes markdownlint validation with zero violations.

## Core Principles

### 1. Blank Lines Are Mandatory

- Before/after ALL lists (MD032)
- Before/after ALL headings except document start (MD022)
- Before/after ALL code blocks (MD031)
- Between ALL block-level elements

### 2. Consistency Required

- Use `-` for lists
- Use `#` for headings (ATX)
- Regular spaces only—never tabs/nbsp

### 3. Structure Matters

- Heading hierarchy: 1→2→3 (not 1→3)
- ONE H1 per document
- Files end with one newline
- Lines under 80 chars

### 4. Invisible Characters Matter

- Use ONLY regular spaces (U+0020)
- Never non-breaking spaces (U+00A0,  )
- Never tabs
- UTF-8 encoding

## Pre-Generation Checklist

- [ ] Where will lists/headings/code appear?
- [ ] Heading levels verified (1→2→3)?
- [ ] Using `-` for all lists?
- [ ] Code languages specified?
- [ ] Lines under 80 chars?
- [ ] Line breaks needed? (two trailing spaces)
- [ ] Using regular spaces only?
- [ ] URLs wrapped in `<>` or `[]`?
- [ ] Document starts with H1?
- [ ] Ordered lists use `1.` for all items?
- [ ] File ends with single newline?
- [ ] Tables use consistent spacing?

## Essential Rules

### Lists (MD032, MD004)

```markdown
Text before.

- Item one
- Item two

Text after.
```

### Headings (MD001, MD022)

```markdown
Text.

## Heading

Content.
```

### Code Blocks (MD031, MD040)

````markdown
Text.

```python
code()
```

Text.
````

**Nested Fences:** When showing markdown examples that contain code blocks,
use **one more backtick** than the deepest level:

- Three backticks (` ``` `): Regular code
- Four backticks (` ```` `): Markdown examples with code
- Five backticks (` ````` `): Nested markdown examples

`````markdown
````markdown
# Example

```bash
command
```

````
`````

### Line Length (MD013)

Break long lines at natural points. Use reference-style links for long URLs.

### URLs and Email (MD034)

Wrap bare URLs and emails:

```markdown
Wrong: https://example.com
Right: <https://example.com>
Right: [link](https://example.com)

Wrong: user@example.com
Right: <user@example.com>
```

### Document Structure (MD041)

Start with H1 (or front matter then H1):

```markdown
# Document Title

First paragraph.
```

### Ordered Lists (MD029)

Use `1.` for all items:

```markdown
1. First
1. Second
1. Third
```

### File Endings (MD047)

End with single newline:

```text
Last content line.
[single newline]
[EOF]
```

### Table Column Style (MD060)

Use consistent spacing in tables. Three styles:

**Compact (recommended):** `| cell |` - single space around content

```markdown
| Header 1 | Header 2 |
| --- | --- |
| Data | More data |
```

**Aligned:** Pipes vertically aligned with padding

**Tight:** `|cell|` - no spaces

Pick ONE style per document. Compact is preferred.

### Character Encoding

**Detection:** View → Render Whitespace in VS Code

**Fix:** Find `\u00A0` → Replace with space

**Critical for AI:** Two trailing spaces = intentional line breaks. Do NOT
remove them.

## Critical Error Patterns

### 1. List Without Blank Lines

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD032 -->

**Wrong:**

```markdown
Text:
- Item
Text.
```

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD032 -->

**Right:**

```markdown
Text:

- Item

Text.
```

### 2. Heading Without Blank Lines

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD022 -->

**Wrong:**

```markdown
Text.
## Head
Text.
```

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD022 -->

**Right:**

```markdown
Text.

## Head

Text.
```

### 3. Code Without Blanks/Language

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD031 MD040 -->

**Wrong:**

````markdown
Text:
```
code
```
Text.
````

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD031 MD040 -->

**Right:**

````markdown
Text:

```python
code
```

Text.
````

### 4. Inconsistent Markers

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD004 -->

**Wrong:**

```markdown
- Item
* Item
```

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD004 -->

**Right:**

```markdown
- Item
- Item
```

### 5. Skipping Levels

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD001 -->

**Wrong:**

```markdown
# Title

### Sub (skipped H2)
```

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD001 -->

**Right:**

```markdown
# Title

## Section

### Sub
```

## Post-Generation Validation

1. Lists have blank lines before/after
2. Headings have blank lines before/after
3. Code has blank lines before/after
4. Heading progression: 1→2→3→4
5. All lists use `-`
6. All code has language
7. Lines under 80 chars
8. Document starts with H1
9. URLs wrapped properly
10. Ordered lists use `1.`
11. File ends with one newline
12. Two trailing spaces used intentionally
13. Only regular spaces (no nbsp/tabs)
14. Tables use consistent column spacing

## Mental Model

Markdown is **blocks with mandatory spacing:**

```text
[Text Block]
↓ BLANK LINE ↓
[Heading Block]
↓ BLANK LINE ↓
[List Block]
↓ BLANK LINE ↓
[Code Block]
↓ BLANK LINE ↓
[Text Block]
[EOF]
```

Every block transition = blank line required.

## Quick Patterns

**List:**

```markdown
text

- item

text
```

**Heading:**

```markdown
text

## Head

text
```

**Code:**

````markdown
text

```lang
code
```

text
````

**Nested:**

```markdown
- parent
  - child
- parent
```

**Ordered:**

```markdown
text

1. item
1. item

text
```

**Table:**

```markdown
text

| Header | Header |
| --- | --- |
| Cell | Cell |

text
```

## Common Languages

**Programming:** `python` `javascript` `java` `c` `cpp` `go` `rust` `ruby`
`php` `swift` `kotlin` `typescript`

**Shell:** `bash` `sh` `powershell` `cmd` `zsh`

**Markup:** `html` `css` `xml` `json` `yaml` `toml` `markdown`

**Database:** `sql` `postgresql` `mysql`

**Other:** `text` `diff` `log`

## Validation

```bash
markdownlint filename.md
```

Goal: Zero errors/warnings.

## Additional Resources

See bundled references:

- `references/complete-rules.md` - Full rule catalog
- `references/edge-cases.md` - Platform quirks
- `references/examples.md` - Detailed examples

## Remember

Most common: Missing blank lines around lists/headings/code.

**Two trailing spaces:** Intentional line breaks. Do NOT remove.

When in doubt:

1. Add blank lines before/after blocks
2. Use `-` for lists
3. Use `#` for headings
4. Specify code language
5. Increment headings by one
6. Use regular spaces only
7. Two trailing spaces = line break

# Swift grammar refresh for entire-graph: design

Status: draft for Rod's review, 2026-10-21. Tracks
<https://github.com/entireio/entire-graph/issues/345>.

## Intent and why

entire-graph parses Swift with the tree-sitter-swift grammar that ships
inside `github.com/smacker/go-tree-sitter`. That library has been dormant
since 2024-08-27, and its latest commit is the one entire-graph pins.
The bundled grammar is tree-sitter-swift 0.5.0. It cannot parse
Swift Testing's freestanding macros (`#expect`, `#require`), along with
other Swift 5.9 to 6 syntax. As a result, most Swift test files, and
some source files, become `E_PARSE_ERROR` partial failures. Graph then
holds incomplete facts for them, and `entire brain doctor` reports them
as semantic blind spots.

Rod wants two outcomes from one piece of work:

1. A locally built binary that he installs and judges by
   `entire brain doctor` in his own Swift app ("fewer complaints").
1. A patch offered upstream that is small and well evidenced, which
   raises the chance that the maintainers act on #345.

Rod is an outside contributor, not a maintainer. The patch has to look
like something the maintainers would have written themselves.

## Evidence so far

Measured on 2026-10-21 against Rod's private macOS app, which is the
local yardstick only and must never be named or quoted upstream. Each
binary was built from `main` at `dd212259` and run as
`snapshot --worktree --profile full --format ndjson`. Counts are Swift
entries in the summary record's `partial_failures`.

| Binary | Swift files failing | Symbols |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `main` (grammar 0.5.0) | 139 | 8,530 |
| Grammar 0.7.4 | 19 | 8,655 |
| 0.7.4, leading-operator mask off | 8 | 8,660 |
| 0.7.4, all Swift masking off | 8 | 8,660 |

None of the variants broke a file that parses on `main`. The 8 that
remain are gaps in the grammar itself:

- Regex literals containing `{n,m}` or `\/` (4 files)
- `any Error` inside a tuple type argument
- `final` used as an identifier
- `while await !x`
- One cascade from line 1 whose cause is unknown

An earlier session (2026-10-14) measured hummingbird 2.28.0,
OnionBrowser v3.4.3 and firefox-ios firefox-v158.0, and found two
regressions in 0.7.4:

- A lone attribute inside `#if` directly above a declaration (19
  uniffi-generated firefox-ios files)
- `switch consume self.state`, which fails a whole hummingbird file

## Precedent upstream

- 11 grammars are already vendored under `internal/sem/grammars/<lang>`
  (Dart, Clojure, C#, Erlang, F#, Haskell, Julia, Objective-C, Perl, R,
  Zig). Each has `binding.go`, `LICENSE`, `parser.c`, `scanner.c` (where
  the grammar has one) and a `tree_sitter/` header directory, and each
  is listed in `NOTICES`.
- 10 of them are languages smacker never had. **C# is the exception and
  the exact precedent:** commit `2388fa8e` (PR #21, checkpoint
  `60eb72eb08f4`) replaced smacker's stale C# grammar with a vendored
  tree-sitter-c-sharp v0.23.5. It regenerated `parser.c` with
  tree-sitter-cli 0.24.7 `--abi 14` for smacker's ABI-14 runtime,
  dropped masks the new grammar made unnecessary, kept or added others,
  and reported before and after parse-failure counts.
- Grammar provenance (repo, tag, ABI) is recorded only in commit
  messages. Nothing records the exact source revision of each vendored
  grammar, and there is no tooling to refresh one.
- Language promotions report "score-neutral on all 21 scored
  repositories", which tells us what evidence the maintainers expect.

## Goals

- Swift is parsed by tree-sitter-swift 0.7.4 (the newest
  `-with-generated-files` tag at ABI 14), vendored at
  `internal/sem/grammars/swift`, the same way C# was.
- A manifest records, for every vendored grammar, its source repository,
  tag or ref, exact commit and ABI.
- A refresh script fetches a named grammar at a given ref into
  `internal/sem/grammars/<lang>` and updates the manifest. Swift is its
  first real use, so the script is proven by the change itself.
- Masks that the new grammar makes harmful or unnecessary are removed.
- `IdentityRevision` is bumped in the same commit as the grammar swap.
- Evidence for upstream: before and after Swift parse-failure counts on
  the three public repos, plus the maintainers' scored benchmark set
  showing no meaningful score loss.
- A local binary Rod installs, then checks with `entire brain doctor` in
  his app.

## Non-goals

- Refreshing any other grammar now. The script should make that easy
  later; doing it is out of scope.
- Replacing smacker's core runtime or moving to the official
  `tree-sitter/go-tree-sitter` bindings.
- Fixing the 8 remaining grammar gaps inside entire-graph. They may be
  reported to tree-sitter-swift separately, as a later choice.
- Downloading anything during `go build` or at runtime. The script is
  run by a maintainer and its output is committed.
- The stray `.cue` fixture parse failure seen in Rod's app.

## Anti-goals

- Anything from Rod's private app (its name, paths or code) appearing in
  the upstream patch, issue comments, commit messages or test fixtures.
- Hiding regressions. Rod accepts a few regressions **only if they are
  reported honestly** in the PR, with counts and examples.
- Shipping the grammar swap without the `IdentityRevision` bump. The
  caches are keyed on the git tree, so users would keep stale results
  and the fix would be invisible.
- Forking smacker or adding a new third-party Go dependency.
- Machinery heavy enough that the maintainers would rather reject it.
  The script must stay small, and the Swift swap must make sense on its
  own if they keep it but drop the script.

## Constraints

- Contract rules in `AGENTS.md`: schema `1.x` additive-only, no egress,
  stable `compound-v1` IDs (hence the `IdentityRevision` bump), and
  unparseable files surface as partial failures.
- smacker's runtime accepts grammar ABI 13 to 14 only. A grammar built
  for ABI 15 must be regenerated with `--abi 14` (the C# technique) or
  refused by the script with a clear message.
- tree-sitter-swift 0.7.4's generated `parser.c` is about 23 MB. That's
  normal for this repo's vendored grammars, but it makes for a large diff.
- Licences: copy the grammar's `LICENSE` and regenerate `NOTICES` with
  `scripts/gen-notices.sh`.
- `go test -race` on `internal/sem` is too slow for a full run (Brain
  gotcha). Scope test runs and say what was not run.
- Rod's rules: work on a branch, never `main`. No PR, comment or issue
  is posted without Rod's express approval, and anything attributed to
  him says upfront that an agent wrote it under his direction.

## Decided with Rod

- The new grammar is vendored into the repo, not taken from a smacker
  fork and not pulled at build time.
- A manifest plus refresh script is added, with Swift first.
- A few regressions are acceptable if reported honestly.
- Design and plan documents stay in the session scratchpad, never in
  the repo.

## My calls (for Rod to check)

- **Manifest format and location:** a small JSON file at
  `internal/sem/grammars/grammars.json`, shaped like smacker's
  `_automation/grammars.json` (language, url, files, reference, revision)
  plus `abi`. This reuses a format the maintainers have already seen.
- **Script language:** Go, run with `go run`, under `scripts/` or
  `internal/sem/grammars/`, whichever reads more naturally next to the
  existing scripts. Go needs no extra toolchain; smacker's updater is Go
  too.
- **Backfilling the other 11 grammars:** add manifest entries for any
  whose source commit can be pinned down reliably from the commit
  messages and upstream tags. Leave the rest out rather than guess, and
  say which in the PR.
- **Masks:** remove the leading-operator continuation mask. Check every
  other Swift mask in `maskSwiftUnsupportedSyntax` one at a time against
  the three public repos and Rod's app. Remove the ones the new grammar
  makes unnecessary, and keep any that still help.
- **Regressions:** don't add new masks for the `#if` attribute or
  `switch consume` cases unless a mask is small and clearly safe. Report
  them in the PR, and link any upstream tree-sitter-swift issue.
- **Commits:** separate commits for (1) manifest plus script, (2) Swift
  swap plus `IdentityRevision` bump plus `NOTICES`, (3) mask removals,
  so the maintainers can take the pieces separately.
- **Local install:** build from the branch and install with
  `scripts/install-local.sh` (the `mise run install` task). Then run
  `entire brain doctor` in Rod's app and compare it with the baseline
  output Rod shared today.

## Left to the builder

- The exact script interface and how it handles a grammar that lacks
  `scanner.c` or ships extra headers.
- Whether the script regenerates from `grammar.js` (needs
  tree-sitter-cli) or only copies pre-generated files. Copying is enough
  for Swift, because the `-with-generated-files` tags contain them.
  Regeneration can be a documented manual step.
- Tests: a Swift extraction test covering at least `#expect` and typed
  throws, plus updates to any tests that pin Swift parse behaviour or
  mask behaviour.
- Which benchmark command produces the "21 scored repositories" result
  (see `bench/README.md`) and how long it takes.
- Wording of the PR description, drafted for Rod's review and not
  posted.

some source files, become `E_PARSE_ERROR` partial failures. Graph then
holds incomplete facts for them, and `entire brain doctor` reports them
as semantic blind spots.

1. A locally built binary that he installs and judges by
   `entire brain doctor` in his own Swift app ("fewer complaints").
1. A patch offered upstream that is small and well evidenced, which
   raises the chance that the maintainers act on #345.

like something the maintainers would have written themselves.

entries in the summary record's `partial_failures`.

| Binary | Swift files failing | Symbols |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `main` (grammar 0.5.0) | 139 | 8,530 |
| Grammar 0.7.4 | 19 | 8,655 |
| 0.7.4, leading-operator mask off | 8 | 8,660 |
| 0.7.4, all Swift masking off | 8 | 8,660 |

# Swift grammar refresh for entire-graph: design

Status: draft for Rod's review, 2026-10-21. Tracks
<https://github.com/entireio/entire-graph/issues/345>.

## Intent and why

entire-graph parses Swift with the tree-sitter-swift grammar that ships
inside `github.com/smacker/go-tree-sitter`. That library has been dormant
since 2024-08-27, and its latest commit is the one entire-graph pins.
The bundled grammar is tree-sitter-swift 0.5.0. It cannot parse
Swift Testing's freestanding macros (`#expect`, `#require`), along with
other Swift 5.9 to 6 syntax. As a result, most Swift test files, and
some source files, become `E_PARSE_ERROR` partial failures. Graph then
holds incomplete facts for them, and `entire brain doctor` reports them
as semantic blind spots.

Rod wants two outcomes from one piece of work:

1. A locally built binary that he installs and judges by
   `entire brain doctor` in his own Swift app ("fewer complaints").
1. A patch offered upstream that is small and well evidenced, which
   raises the chance that the maintainers act on #345.

Rod is an outside contributor, not a maintainer. The patch has to look
like something the maintainers would have written themselves.

## Evidence so far

Measured on 2026-10-21 against Rod's private macOS app, which is the
local yardstick only and must never be named or quoted upstream. Each
binary was built from `main` at `dd212259` and run as
`snapshot --worktree --profile full --format ndjson`. Counts are Swift
entries in the summary record's `partial_failures`.

| Binary | Swift files failing | Symbols |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `main` (grammar 0.5.0) | 139 | 8,530 |
| Grammar 0.7.4 | 19 | 8,655 |
| 0.7.4, leading-operator mask off | 8 | 8,660 |
| 0.7.4, all Swift masking off | 8 | 8,660 |

None of the variants broke a file that parses on `main`. The 8 that
remain are gaps in the grammar itself:

- Regex literals containing `{n,m}` or `\/` (4 files)
- `any Error` inside a tuple type argument
- `final` used as an identifier
- `while await !x`
- One cascade from line 1 whose cause is unknown

An earlier session (2026-10-14) measured hummingbird 2.28.0,
OnionBrowser v3.4.3 and firefox-ios firefox-v158.0, and found two
regressions in 0.7.4:

- A lone attribute inside `#if` directly above a declaration (19
  uniffi-generated firefox-ios files)
- `switch consume self.state`, which fails a whole hummingbird file

## Precedent upstream

- 11 grammars are already vendored under `internal/sem/grammars/<lang>`
  (Dart, Clojure, C#, Erlang, F#, Haskell, Julia, Objective-C, Perl, R,
  Zig). Each has `binding.go`, `LICENSE`, `parser.c`, `scanner.c` (where
  the grammar has one) and a `tree_sitter/` header directory, and each
  is listed in `NOTICES`.
- 10 of them are languages smacker never had. **C# is the exception and
  the exact precedent:** commit `2388fa8e` (PR #21, checkpoint
  `60eb72eb08f4`) replaced smacker's stale C# grammar with a vendored
  tree-sitter-c-sharp v0.23.5. It regenerated `parser.c` with
  tree-sitter-cli 0.24.7 `--abi 14` for smacker's ABI-14 runtime,
  dropped masks the new grammar made unnecessary, kept or added others,
  and reported before and after parse-failure counts.
- Grammar provenance (repo, tag, ABI) is recorded only in commit
  messages. Nothing records the exact source revision of each vendored
  grammar, and there is no tooling to refresh one.
- Language promotions report "score-neutral on all 21 scored
  repositories", which tells us what evidence the maintainers expect.

## Goals

- Swift is parsed by tree-sitter-swift 0.7.4 (the newest
  `-with-generated-files` tag at ABI 14), vendored at
  `internal/sem/grammars/swift`, the same way C# was.
- A manifest records, for every vendored grammar, its source repository,
  tag or ref, exact commit and ABI.
- A refresh script fetches a named grammar at a given ref into
  `internal/sem/grammars/<lang>` and updates the manifest. Swift is its
  first real use, so the script is proven by the change itself.
- Masks that the new grammar makes harmful or unnecessary are removed.
- `IdentityRevision` is bumped in the same commit as the grammar swap.
- Evidence for upstream: before and after Swift parse-failure counts on
  the three public repos, plus the maintainers' scored benchmark set
  showing no meaningful score loss.
- A local binary Rod installs, then checks with `entire brain doctor` in
  his app.

## Non-goals

- Refreshing any other grammar now. The script should make that easy
  later; doing it is out of scope.
- Replacing smacker's core runtime or moving to the official
  `tree-sitter/go-tree-sitter` bindings.
- Fixing the 8 remaining grammar gaps inside entire-graph. They may be
  reported to tree-sitter-swift separately, as a later choice.
- Downloading anything during `go build` or at runtime. The script is
  run by a maintainer and its output is committed.
- The stray `.cue` fixture parse failure seen in Rod's app.

## Anti-goals

- Anything from Rod's private app (its name, paths or code) appearing in
  the upstream patch, issue comments, commit messages or test fixtures.
- Hiding regressions. Rod accepts a few regressions **only if they are
  reported honestly** in the PR, with counts and examples.
- Shipping the grammar swap without the `IdentityRevision` bump. The
  caches are keyed on the git tree, so users would keep stale results
  and the fix would be invisible.
- Forking smacker or adding a new third-party Go dependency.
- Machinery heavy enough that the maintainers would rather reject it.
  The script must stay small, and the Swift swap must make sense on its
  own if they keep it but drop the script.

## Constraints

- Contract rules in `AGENTS.md`: schema `1.x` additive-only, no egress,
  stable `compound-v1` IDs (hence the `IdentityRevision` bump), and
  unparseable files surface as partial failures.
- smacker's runtime accepts grammar ABI 13 to 14 only. A grammar built
  for ABI 15 must be regenerated with `--abi 14` (the C# technique) or
  refused by the script with a clear message.
- tree-sitter-swift 0.7.4's generated `parser.c` is about 23 MB. That's
  normal for this repo's vendored grammars, but it makes for a large diff.
- Licences: copy the grammar's `LICENSE` and regenerate `NOTICES` with
  `scripts/gen-notices.sh`.
- `go test -race` on `internal/sem` is too slow for a full run (Brain
  gotcha). Scope test runs and say what was not run.
- Rod's rules: work on a branch, never `main`. No PR, comment or issue
  is posted without Rod's express approval, and anything attributed to
  him says upfront that an agent wrote it under his direction.

## Decided with Rod

- The new grammar is vendored into the repo, not taken from a smacker
  fork and not pulled at build time.
- A manifest plus refresh script is added, with Swift first.
- A few regressions are acceptable if reported honestly.
- Design and plan documents stay in the session scratchpad, never in
  the repo.

## My calls (for Rod to check)

- **Manifest format and location:** a small JSON file at
  `internal/sem/grammars/grammars.json`, shaped like smacker's
  `_automation/grammars.json` (language, url, files, reference, revision)
  plus `abi`. This reuses a format the maintainers have already seen.
- **Script language:** Go, run with `go run`, under `scripts/` or
  `internal/sem/grammars/`, whichever reads more naturally next to the
  existing scripts. Go needs no extra toolchain; smacker's updater is Go
  too.
- **Backfilling the other 11 grammars:** add manifest entries for any
  whose source commit can be pinned down reliably from the commit
  messages and upstream tags. Leave the rest out rather than guess, and
  say which in the PR.
- **Masks:** remove the leading-operator continuation mask. Check every
  other Swift mask in `maskSwiftUnsupportedSyntax` one at a time against
  the three public repos and Rod's app. Remove the ones the new grammar
  makes unnecessary, and keep any that still help.
- **Regressions:** don't add new masks for the `#if` attribute or
  `switch consume` cases unless a mask is small and clearly safe. Report
  them in the PR, and link any upstream tree-sitter-swift issue.
- **Commits:** separate commits for (1) manifest plus script, (2) Swift
  swap plus `IdentityRevision` bump plus `NOTICES`, (3) mask removals,
  so the maintainers can take the pieces separately.
- **Local install:** build from the branch and install with
  `scripts/install-local.sh` (the `mise run install` task). Then run
  `entire brain doctor` in Rod's app and compare it with the baseline
  output Rod shared today.

## Left to the builder

- The exact script interface and how it handles a grammar that lacks
  `scanner.c` or ships extra headers.
- Whether the script regenerates from `grammar.js` (needs
  tree-sitter-cli) or only copies pre-generated files. Copying is enough
  for Swift, because the `-with-generated-files` tags contain them.
  Regeneration can be a documented manual step.
- Tests: a Swift extraction test covering at least `#expect` and typed
  throws, plus updates to any tests that pin Swift parse behaviour or
  mask behaviour.
- Which benchmark command produces the "21 scored repositories" result
  (see `bench/README.md`) and how long it takes.
- Wording of the PR description, drafted for Rod's review and not
  posted.

- **Commit order:** the Swift swap goes first, then the mask removals, then the manifest and script last. That way upstream can take the swap without the script.
- **When to stop:** a few regressions within a repo that improves overall get reported and shipped. If any public Swift repo comes out worse overall, with more failing files or fewer symbols, I stop and bring it back to you.
- **What I hand over:** a local branch and a drafted PR description. Nothing goes to a fork or GitHub without your say-so.
- **Your baseline:** the `brain doctor` output you pasted came from the released v0.4.0 plugin. I'll take a fresh baseline with the HEAD builds you've just installed before installing the branch.

One question is yours, and it matters more than I'd realised. **Entire records this session, and its transcript goes to the shared repo.** I checked:

- This session is tracked by Entire (`7bfdd797…`).
- `entire/checkpoints/v1` lives on `origin`, which is the entireio mirror.
- Any commit made from this session gets an `Entire-Checkpoint:` trailer. Pushing it publishes the transcript, and upstream maintainers can read those, the way I read the C# one today.

This transcript already names Porter and contains your full `brain doctor` output, including file paths and album fixture names. Every session that measures Porter will contain the same kind of detail.

My suggestion is to split the work into two sessions:

- **Upstream session:** makes the upstream commits. It's a fresh session that never touches Porter and works only with the public repos.
- **Local session:** a separate one, with nothing pushed, for the Porter measurements and your local install.

This session would make no commits at all.

How do you want to handle that? You could use that split, turn checkpoints off for the upstream branch, or tell me you're fine with what gets published.

sem: fix C#/PHP call and definition extraction gaps found by the brain-bench C#/PHP batch
Five extraction bugs diagnosed from the brain-bench C#/PHP significance batch (dotnet/runtime, dotnet/roslyn, laravel/framework, WordPress/wordpress-develop), rebased onto main. Each fix commit carries a regression test.

## C#

1. **Vendor tree-sitter-c-sharp v0.23.5 at ABI 14** (`76d59ec`) — the bundled grammar predates C# 12/13; a single `params ReadOnlySpan<Task>` overload in runtime's `Task.cs` swallowed the enclosing `class Task` and every later member (177 of ~800 symbols). Corpus parse-failure counts: runtime 3920, roslyn 1593, efcore 945, aspnetcore 544. `Task.cs` now parses with zero ERROR nodes; roslyn's failures drop 1593 → 286. Masks for primary constructors and collection expressions are removed (grammar-native now); preprocessor masking stays, plus a new length-preserving mask for `*(T*)&x` pointer-deref casts, the one construct the new grammar still rejects.
2. **Out-declaration / nullable-local receiver types** (`8f9b3e4`) — `out HttpConnectionPool? pool` and `Type? local;` now feed receiver-type inference; parameter modifiers (`out/ref/in/params/this/scoped/readonly`) no longer corrupt signature-derived types.
3. **Static calls across partial classes** (`d01e5aa`) — type-name resolution prefers the partial declaration that actually defines the called method; roslyn's `Contract.ThrowIfFalse(...)` (declared in Contract.cs, shadowed by the lexically-first Contract.InterpolatedStringHandlers.cs) now resolves `type_inferred` 0.82.

## PHP

4. **Closure-body receiver inference** (`cfe0e78`) — an untyped receiver named after the enclosing type resolves to it (method-existence gated): laravel's `Container.getClosure` now emits CALLS to `Container.build` and `Container.resolve`.
5. **Ambiguous bare calls + docblock return types** (`568a423`) — ambiguous name-only calls emit ranked candidate edges instead of silence (WordPress `apply_filters`, 3 declarations); the chained-call regex family accepts `->`; `@return` docblock types drive `rest_get_server()->dispatch()` resolution; nullable `: ?Type` hints are stripped correctly.

Plus `1ec76d0`: regression tests pinning two bugs found by self-measuring the benchmark corpus (jq's C typedef-return misnaming, Go self-module package imports) whose fixes had already landed on main independently.

## Verification

Full `go test ./...` passes on the rebased branch. Brain-bench re-measurement with this binary: roslyn 17/18 → **18/18**, framework 20/21 → **21/21**, wordpress-develop 18/20 → **20/20** (runtime re-measure in flight). Score artifacts land in a separate brain-bench PR, cross-linked here.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

# Semantic Provider Benchmark

`graph-bench` clones popular real-world repositories per language and measures the
semantic provider over them, emitting a machine-readable performance and quality
report. It originated as the WP10 harness in the
[archived v2 implementation plan](../docs/archive/2026-06-18-entire-graph-v2-implementation-plan.md)
and is meant to be re-run each work phase to track regressions and quality gains.

## Design

- **Clone phase (network) is separate from measurement (no-egress).** Cloning
  uses `git`; the measured analysis runs `BuildProviderSnapshot` with
  `NoNetwork` set, so the path we benchmark is the same local-only path the
  provider guarantees in production.
- **Cloned repos never enter our commits.** They live under `bench/.cache/`,
  which is gitignored.
- **Repeatable.** `bench/repos.json` lists the repositories; `bench/repos.lock.json`
  pins each to an exact commit. Commit the lock file so every phase analyzes the
  same source and the numbers are comparable.

## Tiers

| Tier | Manifest               | Repos               | When                                          |
| ---- | ---------------------- | ------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| Fast | `bench/repos.fast.json`| 3/language (72)     | Routine per-phase tracking; runs in minutes.  |
| Full | `bench/repos.json`     | 10/language (240)   | Occasional deep runs; includes mega-repos.    |

The fast tier is a curated subset of the full manifest (no mega-repos like
linux/tensorflow/vscode), so its repos share the same `repos.lock.json` pins and
clone cache — no separate lock needed. The full tier is comprehensive but gated
by a handful of giant repositories and can take 1.5-3 hours.

## Layout

| Path                     | Purpose                                                |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| `bench/repos.json`       | Full manifest: 10 popular repos per language.          |
| `bench/repos.fast.json`  | Fast manifest: 3 repos per language (subset of full).  |
| `bench/repos.lock.json`  | Commit pins for reproducibility (covers both tiers).   |
| `bench/.cache/`          | Cloned repositories (gitignored).                      |

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write implementation plans for an engineer who has not seen this codebase or this spec. Assume they write idiomatic code in the project's language once they know the exact interface and the exact test, and that they will make a reasonable choice wherever the plan leaves one open. What they cannot know is what you decided: which files, which names and signatures, which values from the spec, which tests prove each task. Document those. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** If working in an isolated worktree, it should have been created via the `superpowers:using-git-worktrees` skill at execution time.

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Task Right-Sizing

A task is the smallest unit that carries its own test cycle and is worth a
fresh reviewer's gate. When drawing task boundaries: fold setup,
configuration, scaffolding, and documentation steps into the task whose
deliverable needs them; split only where a reviewer could meaningfully
reject one task while approving its neighbor. Each task ends with an
independently testable deliverable.

## Step Granularity

**Each step is one action with a checkable result:**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

**Spec:** [path to the spec/design doc this plan implements — the plan
argues from the spec, so the spec travels with it; executors read both]

## Global Constraints

[The spec's project-wide requirements — version floors, dependency limits,
naming and copy rules, platform requirements — one line each, with exact
values copied verbatim from the spec. Every task's requirements implicitly
include this section.]

## Review Focus

[The five input classes or failure modes the spec implies but no task's
tests exercise that are most likely to bite a person using this software
— one line each, naming the input or condition and the behavior a
reasonable person would expect, most likely first. The spec is a vision
document: it says what the software must do, not everything it will
meet, and its silence on an input is not permission for that input to
break the program. Write the list here, once, with the spec in front of
you. Then, for each line, add the test that pins it to the task that
owns the code, in that task's own step style.]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: [what this task uses from earlier tasks — exact signatures]
- Produces: [what later tasks rely on — exact function names, parameter
  and return types. A task's implementer sees only their own task; this
  block is how they learn the names and types neighboring tasks use.]

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Implement `function(input: InputType) -> ResultType` in `exact/path/to/file.py`**

One line on the approach when the signature and the test leave a choice
(which library call, which data structure); a code block only for an
algorithm they do not determine.

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

## What a Step Contains

A step is done when the implementer can write exactly one reasonable thing
from it. That is the whole requirement: unambiguous, not complete. Each kind
of step carries what makes it unambiguous and nothing more:

- **A test step:** the test's name and its assertions, as code, with the
  spec's exact values in them.
- **A code step:** the exact signature (name, parameters, return type), the
  file it lives in, and the specific values the spec pins. The implementer
  writes the body. A body appears only for an algorithm the signature and
  tests do not determine, or for exact copy the spec fixes.
- **A verification step:** the command to run and the output that means it
  passed.
- **A reference to another task:** that task's Interfaces block says what
  to use; the plan does not repeat that task's code.

A plan is the set of decisions the implementer cannot make alone. A plan
longer than the code it describes has written the code instead. Lines that
decide nothing ("TBD", "handle edge cases", "add appropriate validation",
"write tests for the above", a type or function no task defines) are the
opposite failure, and the self-review catches both.

## Self-Review

After writing the complete plan, look at the spec with fresh eyes and check the plan against it. This is a checklist you run yourself — not a subagent dispatch.

**1. Spec coverage:** Skim each section/requirement in the spec. Can you point to a task that implements it? List any gaps.

**2. Step scan:** Every step must let the implementer write exactly one reasonable thing, and no step may carry more than that: a line that decides nothing is a gap, a function body the signature and tests already determine is a transcript. Fix both.

**3. Type consistency:** Do the types, method signatures, and property names you used in later tasks match what you defined in earlier tasks? A function called `clearLayers()` in Task 3 but `clearFullLayers()` in Task 7 is a bug.

**4. Review Focus:** For each input class or failure mode the spec implies, is there a task whose tests exercise it? The five uncovered ones most likely to bite a person go in the Review Focus section, and each line there gets its test added to the owning task. An empty section means you checked and found none, not that you skipped the check.

**5. Proportion:** Compare the plan's length to the spec's. A plan several times longer than the spec it implements is a transcript of the program, not a plan. If code blocks are most of the document, replace bodies with signatures, test names and assertions, and check that each step is still unambiguous.

If you find issues, fix them inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on. If you find a spec requirement with no task, add the task.

## Execution Handoff

After saving and self-reviewing the plan, link it for your human partner
to read. If they have already explicitly supplied an execution method, ask
them to review the plan and confirm it captures what they want; wait for that
review before implementation, then use the preserved method. Otherwise, ask
them to review the plan and choose an execution method before implementation.

**When no execution method has already been supplied:**

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Please review the plan. Which execution approach would you prefer?**

- **Subagent-driven** - A fresh subagent implements each task and a fresh reviewer checks it before the next one starts, then a whole-branch review at the end. Most thorough; costs a fresh context per task and per review.
- **Native** - I implement every task myself in this session, the way this harness runs work, then one fresh reviewer on the most capable model checks the whole branch. Cheapest and fastest; no independent review until the end. Runs well with a mid-tier session model, since the plan carries the design.

**For this plan I recommend <one of the two>, because <one sentence from the plan: how much the tasks depend on each other's interfaces, how many there are, what a shipped mistake would cost>. Does the plan capture what you want, and which approach should we use?"**

**When an execution method has already been supplied:**

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Please review the plan. Does it capture what you want?"**

**If Subagent-driven chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development

**If Native chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:executing-plans

## graph-bench report partial failures fields usage

### graph-bench report fields > Report
## Report

Each run writes `bench/results/result-<unix>.json` containing, per repository and
aggregated per language and overall:

- **Performance:** wall time, files, lines of code, files/sec, LOC/sec, output
  bytes, Go allocation bytes.
- **Quality:** symbols, relations, relations by type, resolution distribution
  (`exact`/`import_resolved`/`name_only`/…), confidence bands
  (`exact`/`strong`/`heuristic`/`weak`), parse failures by code, and unresolved
  relative imports.

To compare phases, run with the same lock file and diff the `by_language` and
`totals` aggregates between two `result-*.json` files. Quality regressions show
up as shifts in resolution/confidence distributions or rising parse failures;
performance regressions show up as falling LOC/sec or rising wall time.

## graph-bench report partial failures fields usage

### graph-bench report fields > Report
## Report

Each run writes `bench/results/result-<unix>.json` containing, per repository and
aggregated per language and overall:

- **Performance:** wall time, files, lines of code, files/sec, LOC/sec, output
  bytes, Go allocation bytes.
- **Quality:** symbols, relations, relations by type, resolution distribution
  (`exact`/`import_resolved`/`name_only`/…), confidence bands
  (`exact`/`strong`/`heuristic`/`weak`), parse failures by code, and unresolved
  relative imports.

To compare phases, run with the same lock file and diff the `by_language` and
`totals` aggregates between two `result-*.json` files. Quality regressions show
up as shifts in resolution/confidence distributions or rising parse failures;
performance regressions show up as falling LOC/sec or rising wall time.

# Swift Grammar Refresh Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use
> superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or
> superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps
> use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** Parse Swift with a vendored tree-sitter-swift 0.7.4 instead of
smacker's bundled 0.5.0, drop the masks it makes harmful or unnecessary,
and add a manifest plus refresh tool for all vendored grammars.

**Architecture:** Follow the C# precedent (commit `76d59ec0`, PR #21):
vendor the grammar under `internal/sem/grammars/swift` and switch the
`.swift` entry in `internal/sem/parser.go` to it. smacker remains the
runtime for every language. A small Go command records and refreshes
vendored grammars from `internal/sem/grammars/grammars.json`.

**Tech Stack:** Go with cgo, smacker/go-tree-sitter runtime (ABI 13 to
14), tree-sitter-swift `0.7.4-with-generated-files`, `graph-bench`.

**Spec:**
`/private/tmp/claude-502/-Users-rod-build-entire-graph/7bfdd797-ea5f-4338-80e4-17ab056773fd/scratchpad/2026-10-21-swift-grammar-refresh-design.md`

## Global Constraints

- Branch `fix/345-swift-grammar-refresh` off `main` at `dd212259` or
  later, in a git worktree. Never commit to `main`. Do not touch the
  primary checkout's uncommitted `.claude/settings.json`.
- Plan and notes stay in the scratchpad. Nothing under `docs/superpowers`
  in the repo.
- Commit order: (1) Swift swap, (2) leading-operator mask, (3) other mask
  removals, (4) manifest plus tool. Each commit must build and pass
  `go test ./internal/sem` on its own.
- Commit subjects use the `sem(swift):` prefix (`sem(grammars):` for
  commit 4). Bodies state the problem with a concrete repro and corpus
  counts, then the fix. Each ends with
  `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`.
- `IdentityRevision` goes from `"4"` to `"5"` in commit 1.
- No egress in the provider. Only the maintainer tool and `graph-bench`
  touch the network.
- Grammars must be ABI 13 or 14 (`#define LANGUAGE_VERSION`).
- Run `gofmt -s`, `go vet ./...` and `scripts/gen-notices.sh --check`
  before each commit. Skip `go test -race` on `internal/sem`, which is
  too slow (30 min timeout), and say so in the PR.
- Evidence of record: the 10 Swift repos in `bench/repos.json`, run via
  `go run ./cmd/graph-bench -languages Swift`. Secondary: hummingbird
  2.28.0, OnionBrowser v3.4.3, firefox-ios firefox-v158.0, and Porter
  (`~/build/porter`).
- Stop and report to Rod if any benchmark Swift repo comes out net worse
  (more parse failures or fewer symbols) than baseline.
- Push only to <https://github.com/rodbegbie/entire-graph>. Never open a
  PR or comment on entireio without Rod's express approval.

## Review Focus

- A grammar ref without generated sources (no `src/parser.c`): the tool
  must fail with a message naming the ref and the missing file, not
  vendor a partial grammar. Pinned in Task 5.
- An ABI 15 grammar: the tool must refuse, saying the runtime accepts 13
  to 14 and suggesting `tree-sitter generate --abi 14`. Pinned in Task 5.
- A grammar with no `scanner.c`, or a refresh after the scanner was
  dropped upstream: no stale `scanner.c` may remain in the directory.
  Pinned in Task 5.
- Re-running the tool at the same ref must produce no diff, including
  manifest key order and trailing newline. Pinned in Task 5, and in
  Task 6 against the committed Swift grammar.
- Users with a warm cache from revision 4 must not be served old Swift
  symbols. Pinned by the revision test in Task 2.

---

### Task 1: Worktree and baselines

**Files:**
- Create (scratchpad only): `baseline/bench-swift-main.json`,
  `baseline/porter-doctor-head.txt`, `baseline/secondary-main.json`

**Interfaces:**
- Produces: the baseline files that Tasks 3, 4 and 7 compare against.

- [ ] **Step 1:** Use superpowers:using-git-worktrees to create branch
  `fix/345-swift-grammar-refresh` in a worktree. Then run
  `entire session adopt <session-id> --from /Users/rod/build/entire-graph`
  so commits get checkpoints (AGENTS.md, "Working in a scratch worktree").
- [ ] **Step 2:** In the worktree, run
  `go run ./cmd/graph-bench -languages Swift -out <scratchpad>/baseline/bench-swift-main.json`.
  Expected: 10 Swift repos measured. Record per-repo parse failures and
  symbols in a small table in `<scratchpad>/notes.md`.
- [ ] **Step 3:** In `~/build/porter`, run
  `entire brain doctor > <scratchpad>/baseline/porter-doctor-head.txt 2>&1`
  using the HEAD plugin Rod installed. Record the `semantic:` summary line.
- [ ] **Step 4:** Build `main` to `<scratchpad>/eg-main`. Run
  `snapshot --worktree --profile full --format ndjson` over the three
  secondary repos at their pinned tags (clone into
  `<scratchpad>/secondary/`). Save Swift partial-failure counts and
  symbol counts per repo to `baseline/secondary-main.json`.

### Task 2: Vendor tree-sitter-swift 0.7.4 (commit 1)

**Files:**
- Create: `internal/sem/grammars/swift/{binding.go,parser.c,scanner.c,LICENSE}`
- Create: `internal/sem/grammars/swift/tree_sitter/{alloc.h,array.h,parser.h}`
- Modify: `internal/sem/parser.go:46` (import) and `:122` (`.swift` entry)
- Modify: `internal/sem/provider.go:63` (`IdentityRevision`) and its
  revision comment
- Modify: `internal/sem/identity_revision_test.go`, `NOTICES`
- Test: `internal/sem/swift_test.go`

**Interfaces:**
- Produces: package `swift` at
  `github.com/entireio/entire-graph/internal/sem/grammars/swift` with
  `func GetLanguage() *sitter.Language`.

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing tests** in `internal/sem/swift_test.go`:
  - `TestSwiftTestingMacrosParse` parses an `@Test func` body containing
    `#expect(value == 3)` and `let x = try #require(optional)`. Assert
    `language == "Swift"`, `!status.ParseError`, and that an entity
    named for the test function exists.
  - `TestSwiftGrammarRefreshIsRevisioned` in
    `identity_revision_test.go`, following
    `TestRemainingNestedCallableCorrectionsAreRevisioned`: assert
    `IdentityRevision != "4"`. Also change the `"4"` in
    `TestParserIdentityRevisionsSnapshotAndCaches` to `"5"`.
- [ ] **Step 2:** Run
  `go test ./internal/sem -run 'TestSwiftTestingMacrosParse|Revision'`.
  Expected: FAIL (ParseError on `#expect`; revision still 4).
- [ ] **Step 3: Vendor the grammar.** Shallow-clone
  `https://github.com/alex-pinkus/tree-sitter-swift` at tag
  `0.7.4-with-generated-files` (commit
  `82bb3a533e0801fd2bbaa11dc49676e10bf41948`). Copy `src/parser.c`
  (already ABI 14; identical to `src/parser_abi14.c`), `src/scanner.c`,
  `src/tree_sitter/*.h` and `LICENSE`, unmodified. Copy the files
  verbatim: don't rewrite the includes the way smacker's updater does.
  Write `binding.go` like `grammars/csharp/binding.go`. It calls
  `tree_sitter_swift()`, and its doc comment says "v0.7.4, ABI 14,
  replacing the 0.5.0 grammar bundled with go-tree-sitter so Swift
  5.9–6 syntax (freestanding macros such as `#expect`) parses".
- [ ] **Step 4:** Point `.swift` at the vendored package, and remove the
  smacker `swift` import. Set `IdentityRevision = "5"`, adding a
  "Revision 5:" comment in the existing style. It should say that the
  refreshed Swift grammar changes which declarations are extracted from
  previously failing files, so cached revision-4 records must not be
  served. Run `scripts/gen-notices.sh`.
- [ ] **Step 5:** Run `go test ./internal/sem`. Expected: PASS. Fix any
  Swift test that pinned 0.5.0 behaviour only if the new behaviour is
  correct, and list each one in `notes.md` for the commit message.
- [ ] **Step 6:** Run `gofmt -s -l internal`, `go vet ./...` and
  `scripts/gen-notices.sh --check`. Expected: no output, exit 0.
- [ ] **Step 7: Commit** with the subject
  `sem(swift): vendor tree-sitter-swift v0.7.4 (Swift 6) at ABI 14`.
  The body follows the C# commit: problem, failure counts (filled in
  from Task 3), and what happened to the masks (none changed yet).
  Amend the counts in after Task 3, before any later commit.

### Task 3: Measure the swap (go/no-go gate)

**Files:** scratchpad only (`after-swap/`)

- [ ] **Step 1:** Rerun Task 1 Steps 2 and 4 with the branch build into
  `after-swap/`.
- [ ] **Step 2:** Compare per repo against baseline. Expected: no
  benchmark Swift repo has more parse failures or fewer symbols. **If
  any does, stop and report to Rod** with the repo, the counts and three
  example failing files.
- [ ] **Step 3:** List files that newly fail (regressions) with their
  first error detail, including the known `#if` attribute and
  `switch consume` cases. Keep this list for the PR.

### Task 4: Remove the leading-operator mask (commit 2)

**Files:**
- Modify: `internal/sem/parser.go` (the
  `swiftLeadingOperatorContinuationLinePattern` block in
  `maskSwiftUnsupportedSyntax` and the pattern var at about line 1670)
- Test: `internal/sem/swift_test.go`

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**
  `TestSwiftLeadingOperatorContinuationParses`. Take the shape from
  Porter's `Tests/PorterCLITests/ExclusionTests.swift:18`: an `#expect(`
  call spanning lines, whose continuation line starts with `==`. Assert
  no `ParseError`. Write it as a minimal generic example; don't copy
  Porter's code. If the minimal form passes with the mask on, reduce
  from Porter's actual line until it fails, and note why in the test
  comment.
- [ ] **Step 2:** Run it. Expected: FAIL with the mask in place.
- [ ] **Step 3:** Delete the leading-operator branch and its pattern var.
- [ ] **Step 4:** Run `go test ./internal/sem`. Expected: PASS, including
  `TestTreeSitterParserSwiftMasksModernSyntax`, whose `< kSimilarityFloor`
  and `|| !options.isEmpty` lines now parse natively.
- [ ] **Step 5:** Rerun the Swift bench. Expected: parse failures fall or
  stay level in every repo. Record the counts.
- [ ] **Step 6: Commit** with the subject
  `sem(swift): drop the leading-operator continuation mask`. The body
  says the mask blanked continuation lines for the 0.5.0 grammar and
  now deletes closing parens on 0.7.4, with bench counts. Note that it
  relies on commit 1's `IdentityRevision` bump and would need its own
  bump if landed separately.

### Task 5: Evaluate the remaining Swift masks (commit 3)

**Files:**
- Modify: `internal/sem/parser.go` (`maskSwiftUnsupportedSyntax` and the
  helpers it calls)
- Test: `internal/sem/parser_test.go`

The masks to evaluate are:

- `maskSwiftComputedStringPropertyBlock`
- `maskSwiftPropertyWrapperPrefix`
- `maskSwiftEmptyAttributeCalls`
- `swiftTypedThrowsPattern`
- `maskSwiftAsyncForLine`
- `maskSwiftOptionalBindingShorthand`
- `maskSwiftMultilineStringLiteral` (and `maskSwiftChainedDotLines` if
  only it uses it)

- [ ] **Step 1:** For each mask, build a variant with only that mask
  disabled. Run the Swift bench, and Porter's snapshot, against it.
  Record the parse failures and symbols in `notes.md`.
- [ ] **Step 2:** Mark a mask for removal only if disabling it leaves
  every repo with no more failures and no fewer symbols. Keep the rest
  and record why.
- [ ] **Step 3:** Remove the marked masks together. If all are removed,
  also remove the `spec.language == "Swift"` call site.
  `TestTreeSitterParserSwiftMasksModernSyntax` must still pass
  unchanged, which proves the grammar parses that syntax natively.
  Rename it to `TestTreeSitterParserSwiftParsesModernSyntax` only if no
  mask remains.
- [ ] **Step 4:** Run `go test ./internal/sem`, `gofmt` and `vet`.
  Expected: PASS and clean.
- [ ] **Step 5: Commit** with the subject
  `sem(swift): drop masks the v0.7.4 grammar makes unnecessary`. The
  body has a removed-and-kept list with per-mask evidence. If nothing
  qualifies, skip the commit and record that.

### Task 6: Grammar manifest and refresh tool (commit 4)

**Files:**
- Create: `internal/sem/grammars/grammars.json`
- Create: `cmd/grammar-refresh/main.go`, `cmd/grammar-refresh/refresh.go`
- Test: `cmd/grammar-refresh/refresh_test.go`
- Modify: `bench/README.md` is not touched. Add a short
  "Refreshing a vendored grammar" section to `CONTRIBUTING.md`.

**Interfaces:**
- Manifest: a JSON array sorted by `language`. Each entry has:
  - `language`: the directory name under `internal/sem/grammars`
  - `url`
  - `reference`: tag, branch or `npm:<pkg>@<ver>`
  - `revision`: commit SHA, or `""` if unknown
  - `files`
  - `abi`: int
  - `note`: optional, for example
    `"parser.c regenerated with tree-sitter-cli 0.24.7 --abi 14"`

  Encode it with two-space indent and a trailing newline.
- `type Grammar struct` mirrors those fields.
  `func loadManifest(path string) ([]Grammar, error)`.
  `func saveManifest(path string, gs []Grammar) error`.
- `func languageABI(parserC []byte) (int, error)` reads
  `#define LANGUAGE_VERSION N`.
- `func vendor(srcRoot, destDir string) (files []string, abi int, err error)`
  copies `src/parser.c`, `src/scanner.c` (if present),
  `src/tree_sitter/*.h` and `LICENSE*`/`COPYING*`. It deletes any of
  those files in `destDir` that the source lacks, and never touches
  `binding.go`.
- CLI:
  `go run ./cmd/grammar-refresh -lang <name> -ref <ref> [-url <url>]`.
  It shallow-clones (`git clone --depth 1 --branch <ref>`) into a temp
  dir, calls `vendor`, resolves the commit with `git rev-parse HEAD`,
  and updates or inserts the manifest entry. `-url` is required only
  for a new language.

  - `TestManifestRoundTripStable`: load then save leaves the bytes

- [ ] **Step 3:** Implement the interfaces above.

- [ ] **Step 5: Backfill the manifest.** Write all 12 entries from each

**Files:** scratchpad only (`final/`, `pr-description.md`)

The implementation plan is written:
`/private/tmp/claude-502/-Users-rod-build-entire-graph/7bfdd797-ea5f-4338-80e4-17ab056773fd/scratchpad/2026-10-21-swift-grammar-refresh-plan.md`

It has seven tasks, one for each commit plus measuring steps:

1. **Baselines:** create a separate work copy of the repo (a git worktree) on the new branch. Then record "before" numbers from the 10 benchmark Swift repos, the three secondary repos, and `brain doctor` on Porter with your HEAD install.
2. **Commit 1:** copy tree-sitter-swift 0.7.4 into `internal/sem/grammars/swift`, bump `IdentityRevision` to 5, and regenerate `NOTICES`. The tests are written first: an `#expect` / `#require` parse test and a test that the revision was bumped.
3. **Stop-or-go check:** if any benchmark Swift repo comes out worse overall, I stop and come back to you with examples.
4. **Commit 2:** remove the leading-operator mask, with a regression test modelled on the shape of Porter's failing line but not using its code.
5. **Commit 3:** turn off each remaining Swift mask one at a time, and remove only those whose removal leaves no repo worse.
6. **Commit 4:** the manifest, backfilled for all 12 grammars, and the refresh tool. Its tests cover the ABI 15 refusal, a missing `parser.c`, a stale `scanner.c` and a stable manifest. One check: re-running the tool for Swift must change nothing.
7. **Finish:** run the full test suite and the final benchmarks, install the branch on your machine for `brain doctor`, draft the PR description, and push the branch to your fork. No PR gets opened.

Two things came up while I was planning:

- **The 0.7.4 tag already ships an ABI 14 `parser.c`**, so the files can be copied unchanged. smacker's updater rewrites the include lines, so its output differs, and we won't use it.
- **I moved the refresh tool to `cmd/grammar-refresh/`** rather than `scripts/`. It sits next to `cmd/graph-bench`, which is how this repo lays out its Go command-line tools.

There are two ways to run the plan:

- **Subagent-driven:** a fresh agent implements each task and another reviews it before the next one starts.
- **Native:** I do the tasks myself in this session, then a fresh reviewer checks the whole branch at the end.

I recommend native. The tasks run strictly in order, the stop-or-go check depends on numbers carried forward from earlier steps, and nothing gets merged without you, so a mistake is cheap to catch at the end.

Does the plan capture what you want, and which way should we run it?
